assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's model of collateral constraints and credit cycles shows how small shocks are amplified and persist through asset prices and borrowing limits. It is a foundational mechanism in macro-finance and shaped later work on financial frictions, crises and policy. The conceptual advance is clear and has had very wide influence.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 'Credit Cycles' paper is clearly the joint contribution of Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent financial-accelerator and empirical strand, closely tied to Bernanke, who is not listed. Limiting the award to Kiyotaki and Moore keeps the credit clean.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old and extensively confirmed, extended and used in policy models, including after the 2008 crisis. Timing is not an obstacle.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) could count against it.
Direct empirical validation is less clean than the theoretical influence.
I rely on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified citation or attribution details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This research changed how economists and policymakers understand the distributional effects of technology and trade. Its tasks framework and local-labour-market evidence on import competition are credibly identified and have had large academic and policy influence. The empirical design is transparent.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are central to the China-shock evidence. Autor and Katz are central to the skills, tasks and technology literature, which also depends on Acemoglu, Goldin and Levy, among others. Dorn is a real co-author but is left out of this three-person selection.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from the 2000s to the early 2010s and have been replicated and extended. Debate over magnitudes and interpretation continues but does not undercut the main findings.
uncertainties: Dividing credit among Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Katz is difficult.
Acemoglu already received the 2024 prize, and the tasks-technology literature overlaps with his work.
Some findings about the persistence of trade shocks are still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson, Tabellini and Besley built the modern formal and empirical framework for how constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy and development. Their work has fostered a large field and bridges economics and political science. It meets common standards of originality and influence, and the field's research agenda would look very different without it.
assessment.attribution: The core contributions are the Persson-Tabellini constitutional and electoral-rules research program and the Besley-Persson work on state capacity. The trio is a natural group. Acemoglu and Robinson, recognised in 2024, are close in theme but are separate contributors.
assessment.maturity: Work from the 1990s to the 2010s has been extensively tested and extended. The agenda is mature.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity raises a question of thematic proximity and recency.
Some constitutional-effects estimates rest on cross-country identification that is open to challenge.
My own research field is adjacent, so I weighed the evidence by common criteria rather than by field familiarity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gives a tractable, measurable way to quantify how distortions that misallocate inputs across firms explain cross-country income and TFP differences. It reoriented work on growth and development and supplies a practical diagnostic for policy.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central measurement paper. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is the parallel theoretical contribution, and Rogerson is not on the credited list, which weakens a clean award. I propose only Hsieh and Klenow, but Restuccia has a plausible claim.
assessment.maturity: The framework is more than fifteen years old and widely applied, with active critiques of measurement error and the mapping from dispersion to distortions.
uncertainties: The attribution problem with the unlisted Rogerson.
Measurement-error critiques may weaken the quantitative conclusions.
Whether the committee sees the contribution as a method more than a discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The structural demand-estimation methods for differentiated products (BLP) and the dynamic oligopoly framework made empirical industrial organisation a quantitative tool. They are used routinely in merger review, antitrust and regulation, so the influence reaches both science and practice.
assessment.attribution: The BLP contribution (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is distinct and well identified. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin contributed to related strands, so the broader list is large and credit is diffuse. Restricting it to the BLP trio is defensible.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from the 1990s and is firmly established and widely used.
uncertainties: Choosing among Bresnahan, Pakes, Berry and others is contestable.
The work is more a method than a discovery about the economy.
Results depend on parametric structural assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz's heterogeneous-firm trade model recast the field around firm selection and reallocation, supplying a new channel for gains from trade. Helpman and coauthors extended it to firm-level evidence on exports and FDI. It is a clear conceptual advance with large influence.
assessment.attribution: The central model is Melitz (2003). Closely related contributions come from Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and from Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple, so credit is shared and some key contributors are not listed together. The proposed pair covers the core.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation and extension, with ongoing debate over quantitative gains.
uncertainties: Bernard and others with a claim are not on this ballot.
Overlap with candidates B003 and B041 divides the trade field.
Quantitative gains depend on functional-form assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design give a general theory of how a sender optimally shapes information, with applications from regulation to platforms and media. It is theoretically elegant and broadly applicable.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow originated Bayesian persuasion. Bergemann and Morris developed information design and the Bayes correlated equilibrium. Morris's broader work on global games and higher-order beliefs adds to his claim. Four people have plausible claims, so any award would exclude one.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from 2011 and later. The theory is well established, but empirical and practical confirmation is still developing.
uncertainties: Relative recency compared with more established candidates.
Division of credit among four contributors.
Limited direct empirical validation so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run top-income series built from tax data created a new empirical basis for studying inequality. They have reshaped academic and public debate, and the data infrastructure (the World Inequality Database) is lasting. Influence is very high.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez pioneered the top-income series. Zucman's offshore-wealth and wealth-distribution work is more recent and distinct, and Atkinson, who is deceased, was a key early contributor. Credit is clear for the two proposed names.
assessment.maturity: The income-share findings are well established. The conclusions on wealth dynamics and the r>g argument, and the wealth-distribution estimates, are more contested and still evolving.
uncertainties: Methodological criticism of the wealth-concentration estimates and of the theoretical claims.
Whether the committee judges the contribution mainly data work or a theoretical advance.
Saez also appears in B007, which complicates how his credit is divided.
